newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Bomb attacks on Nigerian military, several wounded.
newsitem.headline: Bomb attacks on Nigerian military, several wounded.

text.p: A bomb ripped through an army bus in Nigeria's commercial hub of Lagos on Wednesday, wounding several people. Panic spread after a second explosion.

A Western diplomat said the blasts appeared to have been timed with the rounding up of a three-day conference in the capital Abuja by wives of African leaders on the promotion of peace on the conflict-plagued continent.
"The bombs seem to have been timed to coincide with the Abuja conference even though the women are in no danger from that distance," the senior diplomat said.
A senior police officer at Lagos state command said the first explosion "was quickly followed by another one and there is pandemonium in the area in Yaba".
"The area has been sealed off and all top officers are inspecting the scene," he added.
An army spokesman said: "What we know so far is that there was no loss of lives. It seems to follow the usual pattern of the bomb blasts that we have had recently."
It was the fifth bomb attack in Lagos since December targeting the military, which has ruled politically-volatile Nigeria for 26 out of 36 years of independence from Britain.
"The first blast hit the army bus which was conveying soldiers to work along Herbert Macauley Road and as people rushed there another explosion occurred nearby," said the police officer.
He said the devices were similar to previous ones that had detonated in Nigeria's biggest city of six million, killing three soldiers and wounding dozens.
About a dozen dissidents including Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka have been charged with treason over the bomb explosions at a Lagos magistrate court and a hearing of the case is due next week.
Police have blamed the blasts on the umbrella opposition group, the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) and its foreign based affiliates. NADECO denies any involvement.
Opposition activists have instead urged the government to look elsewhere including among dismissed or retired members of the armed forces for the culprits.
A bomb hit an army bus in Lagos in January killing three soldiers and wounding many.
In December, two bombs exploded within days targeting the military administrator of Lagos state, Colonel Muhammed Marwa, a close aide of military ruler General Sani Abacha.
Nigeria has been in turmoil since a previous military ruler annulled elections in 1993 that would have restored democracy.

Abacha, who seized power in the aftermath of the annulment promises to hand over to a democratically elected president next year but the opposition dismiss his transition to democracy programme as a ruse to perpetuate his rule.
Nigeria is treated as a pariah over its human rights record and the 1995 hanging on murder charges of nine minority rights activists from the Ogoni tribe including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.
